checks.message: Creating a long-lived IAM user
checks.context: IAM users with static credentials are a top source of credential leaks - they never expire and are often committed to git repos or hardcoded in apps. Prefer IAM roles or AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) for human access.

checks.message: Verify the trust policy follows least-privilege
checks.context: A trust policy with a wildcard principal ("AWS": "*") means any AWS account can assume this role. Always scope the Principal to a specific account, service, or ARN.

checks.message: Verify --max-session-duration is not set higher than necessary
checks.context: The default max session duration is 1 hour (3600s). Setting it up to 12 hours (43200s) means a stolen session token remains valid for up to 12 hours with no way to invalidate it short of deleting the role. Set the shortest duration your workload can tolerate.

checks.message: Attaching AdministratorAccess - full AWS access granted
checks.context: AdministratorAccess is the most powerful policy in AWS. If this role is ever compromised, the attacker owns your entire account. Grant only the specific actions and resources the role actually needs.

checks.message: Attaching PowerUserAccess - near-full AWS access granted
checks.context: PowerUserAccess grants access to almost all AWS services except IAM and Organizations. This is still extremely broad and violates least-privilege. Scope permissions to only what is needed.

checks.message: Attaching AdministratorAccess directly to a user
checks.context: Granting a user full admin access creates a permanent high-privilege identity. If the user's credentials are compromised, the attacker has unrestricted access to your entire AWS account.

checks.message: Inline policy attached directly to a user
checks.context: Inline policies are invisible to most auditing tools and can't be reused or reviewed centrally. Use managed policies so permissions are discoverable, auditable, and consistent across your org.

checks.message: Inline policy attached directly to a role
checks.context: Inline policies bypass centralized policy management and are harder to audit. Use customer managed policies instead so permissions can be reviewed, versioned, and reused.

checks.message: Creating long-lived access key
checks.context: Static access keys never expire and are the #1 credential type found in public git repos and data breaches. Use `aws sts assume-role` or IAM Identity Center for short-lived credentials instead.

checks.message: Review policy document for wildcards in Action or Resource
checks.context: Policies with Action:* or Resource:* grant far more permissions than intended. Use the IAM Access Analyzer policy validator to check for overly permissive statements before attaching.

checks.message: Trust policy being updated - verify no wildcard principals are introduced
checks.context: A trust policy with Principal:* allows any entity in the world to attempt to assume this role. This is a critical misconfiguration that can lead to privilege escalation from outside your account.

checks.message: Role deletion is permanent - verify no active workloads depend on it
checks.context: Deleting a role used by EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or ECS tasks will immediately break those workloads. AWS does not warn you about active usage before deletion.

checks.message: User deletion is permanent - ensure access keys and MFA devices are removed first
checks.context: Deleting a user with active access keys or MFA devices can leave orphaned credentials. Deactivate and delete all access keys and MFA devices before deleting the user.

checks.message: Console access enabled for IAM user - ensure MFA is enforced
checks.context: Console passwords without MFA are a significant risk. Enforce MFA via an IAM policy condition (aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true) so the user cannot perform sensitive actions without a second factor.

checks.message: MFA device being deactivated - this reduces account security
checks.context: Deactivating MFA removes a critical layer of protection. Ensure this is intentional and that the user will immediately re-enroll a new MFA device. Never deactivate MFA for the root account.

checks.message: Attaching AdministratorAccess to an IAM group
checks.context: Every user in this group will receive full admin access to your entire AWS account. If any group member's credentials are compromised, the attacker has unrestricted access. Scope permissions to only what is needed.

checks.message: Attaching PowerUserAccess to an IAM group
checks.context: PowerUserAccess grants access to almost all AWS services except IAM and Organizations. Every user in this group inherits these broad permissions. Scope to specific services and actions.

checks.message: Verify the group's policies don't grant more permissions than this user needs
checks.context: Adding a user to a group instantly grants all policies attached to that group. If the group has admin or broad permissions, the user inherits them immediately.

checks.message: New policy versions take effect immediately if set as default - review the policy document carefully
checks.context: A new default policy version changes permissions for every user, role, and group that has this policy attached. A typo granting s3:* or iam:* can expose your entire account.

checks.message: Store the MFA seed securely - do not save the QR code or secret key in plaintext
checks.context: The virtual MFA seed is the secret used to generate TOTP codes. If it's stored in plaintext, S3, or a git repo, anyone with access can generate valid MFA codes and bypass your second factor.

checks.message: Verify no ELBs or CloudFront distributions reference this certificate
checks.context: Deleting a server certificate that's in use by a load balancer or CloudFront causes HTTPS to fail immediately. AWS may prevent deletion if in use, but verify manually.

checks.message: Permissions boundary restricts the maximum permissions - verify it doesn't break existing access
checks.context: A permissions boundary acts as a ceiling. Any existing permissions that exceed the boundary are silently denied. This can break working applications if the boundary is too restrictive.

checks.message: Permissions boundary restricts the maximum permissions - verify it doesn't break existing access
checks.context: A permissions boundary acts as a ceiling. Any existing permissions that exceed the boundary are silently denied. This can break the user's access to resources they currently use.

checks.message: Changing access key status - verify no active workloads depend on this key
checks.context: Setting an access key to Inactive causes immediate authentication failures for any application, CI/CD pipeline, or script using it. Verify the key is not in use or that a replacement key is configured before changing status.

checks.message: Verify you are not weakening the password policy - minimum length, complexity, and rotation should meet your compliance requirements
checks.context: Weakening the password policy (shorter passwords, no complexity, no rotation) creates a compliance violation and makes brute-force attacks easier. CIS Benchmark requires minimum 14 characters with complexity.

checks.message: Updating a login profile sets a new console password - verify this is authorized
checks.context: Anyone who can call update-login-profile can reset another user's console password without knowing the old one. This is effectively a privilege escalation path if not audited.

checks.message: Updating the SAML metadata changes the trust relationship for federated access
checks.context: An incorrect or malicious SAML metadata document can redirect authentication to an attacker-controlled IdP, allowing unauthorized access to your AWS account via federation.

checks.message: The private key is passed on the command line - ensure it's not logged in shell history
checks.context: The private key appears in your shell history and process list. Clear your shell history after uploading and consider using ACM instead, which manages keys securely.

checks.message: Verify the SSH public key is for CodeCommit access only - not a general-purpose key
checks.context: IAM SSH keys are used for CodeCommit authentication. Using a key that's also used for EC2 or other systems increases the blast radius if the key is compromised.
